title: Geoff Barton, Oracy and the Future of Curriculum Design
author: Chris Jones
summary: Jones reviews 'We Need to Talk', the report of the Commission on the Future of Oracy Education in England chaired by Geoff Barton. He argues that oracy should stand with reading, writing and arithmetic as a foundational entitlement and that the report treats it as both a curriculum outcome and a curriculum method. He sets out its three dimensions of learning to talk, learning through talk and learning about talk, and its link to equity, noting that about a fifth of children are below expected communication levels at the end of Reception. For curriculum leaders he stresses disciplinary talk rather than bolted-on speaking events, mapping the four modes of talk, and protecting expressive arts. He concludes that oracy is a proxy for the quality of education and a distinctly human capability in an age of AI.
points: The report frames oracy as foundational entitlement and as pedagogy, not a standalone initiative or presentation skill.
Three dimensions, learning to, through and about talk, widen oracy from public speaking to understanding language, audience and power.
Strong oracy is disciplinary, so each subject should decide which kinds of talk are intrinsic to its thinking.
Spoken language is unevenly distributed, so oracy is an equity issue rather than enrichment for confident pupils.
quotes: Strong oracy practice is disciplinary. In mathematics, oracy may involve justification, proof and verbal reasoning. In history, it may involve evidential challenge and interpretation.
Collectively, these dimensions position oracy as both a curriculum outcome and a curriculum method.
Oracy is not an enrichment activity for confident pupils. It is a foundational entitlement for every learner.
Vocabulary displayed on classroom walls is not enough. Language must be spoken, rehearsed, applied and refined through purposeful interaction.
In many ways, oracy becomes a proxy for the wider quality of education itself. Strong schools are rarely silent schools.
Because ultimately, curriculum is not simply what pupils receive. It is how they experience participation in learning itself.
